name: JA-16

lead: JA-16 is a laboratory antibody that targets myostatin, a protein that limits how much muscle the body builds.
It is of interest to people chasing a more muscular look, but it is used in animal research rather than as a product for people.

paras: By binding myostatin, the antibody reduces its growth-limiting signal, which in animal models allows muscle to be maintained or increased.
It is not an approved drug and no human trials are listed. Myostatin inhibitors are prohibited by WADA, and online products sold as myostatin blockers are discussed as a concern.

chain: Less brake on muscle growth signalling
angle.text: JA-16 is discussed in physique circles as a route to more muscle by removing myostatin's growth-limiting signal. It remains a laboratory antibody, and discussion centres on animal research.

lead: JA-16 (also written JA16) is an experimental antibody that blocks myostatin, a protein that limits skeletal muscle growth. Interest in it for looks comes from the idea that lowering myostatin activity lets muscle grow larger, giving a fuller, more muscular physique.

It is a research tool used in animal models rather than an approved medicine. Wikipedia's myostatin article mentions that JA-16 maintained overall muscle weight in experimental models of heart failure when myostatin was inhibited [1].
Myostatin inhibition more broadly has produced increased muscle mass in mice and monkeys with other antibodies, and the field has also explored follistatin and activin-receptor approaches [1].

paras: Myostatin is a signalling protein that restrains muscle growth. Antibodies such as JA-16 bind it and reduce its activity, and other myostatin-targeting approaches such as follistatin and soluble activin receptor have raised muscle mass in animals [1].
Myostatin inhibitors are on the WADA prohibited list, and products sold online as myostatin blockers are a topic of discussion in the supplement world [1].
No studies found. Related research on other anti-myostatin antibodies has been done in mice and monkeys [1].
